datatypes.q: What is the difference between primitive and reference types in JavaScript?
datatypes.what:
Primitive variable contains the value itself. When you copy it, a new separate value is created.

Reference variable holds only the address — the actual object resides elsewhere (in the heap). When you copy it, the address is copied, not the object. Two names, one house.
datatypes.analogy:
Primitive = giving someone a photo copy. If they tear their copy, yours remains safe.
Reference = giving the address of a house. If they go and paint the wall, the paint will appear on your house.
datatypes.why: Most JavaScript bugs stem from this — “I made a copy, how did the original change?” And the reason === returns false for objects is the same: it compares the addresses, not the contents.
pros: Passing large objects by reference is cheap — the entire data isn’t copied.
Change it in one place, it appears everywhere (when that’s desired).
Primitives are always safe — copying them poses no risk.
cons: The original can change unintentionally — the most common JS bug.
=== doesn’t work for objects.
You have to remember the difference between shallow and deep copy.
gotchas: [...arr] and {...obj} are shallow — they copy only one level.
Don’t use JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) for deep copy — Dates become strings, undefined disappears.
typeof null returns "object" — a long-standing JavaScript bug that was never fixed.
terms: Simple value — number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint.
Object, array, function — the address (reference) is stored in the variable, not the value itself.
where: “I made a copy, how did the original change?” — the cause in about 90% of cases.
State must be updated immutably — otherwise React doesn’t detect any change.
Objects cannot be compared with === — you need to write a deep comparison.
datatypes.visualCap: Copying a primitive creates a new value. Copying an object copies only the address — both point to the same house.

variables.q: Explain the difference between var, let, and const. When would you use each?
variables.what:
There are three ways to create a variable, and they differ in three aspects: scope, hoisting, and whether they can be changed.

var is old — visible throughout the whole function. let and const are new — visible only within their { } block.
variables.why: var had two problems: it leaked out of if/for blocks, and it allowed redeclaration (which could unintentionally erase the previous value). let/const stopped both.
pros: const makes it clear that the value will not change.
Block scope prevents variable leaks.
Redeclaration is prohibited — the previous value won't be overwritten by mistake.
cons: const does not make an object immutable — the biggest misconception.
Because of the TDZ, using it before declaration throws an error (but that's good).
Older browsers require transpiling for let/const.
gotchas: After const arr = [], arr.push(1) works. const only prevents re-assignment.
var's hoisted value is undefined, while let results in an error.
In the global scope, var x becomes window.x, but let x does not.
terms: The area where the variable is visible.
Assigning a new value to the variable.
Creating a variable again with the same name.
where: Always start with const. Use let only if needed. Never use var.
for (let i...) — a new i each iteration, so closure bugs don’t occur.
In older codebases you’ll find var — you’ll recognize its leak-related bugs.
variables.visualCap: var leaks throughout the entire function; let/const stay only within their block.

When you combine two different types, JS tries to make them the same — whether that makes sense or not.

hoisting.desc: JS moves declarations (not initializations) to the top of their scope before execution.
hoisting.qsub: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
hoisting.what:
Before the code runs, JS scans the entire script once and records all declarations. However, the value is set only where it is written.

Therefore, using var before its declaration yields undefined — the variable exists, but its value has not been assigned.
hoisting.analogy: In a class, the attendance register is created first (all names are written), but students arrive at their own times. The name in the register = declaration. Student not arrived = value undefined.
hoisting.why: Returning var from undefined created silent bugs — the code would run but be incorrect. Therefore, let/const introduced the TDZ: accessing before declaration triggers a error. Bugs appear immediately instead of hiding.
pros: You can write function declarations later and still call them earlier.
TDZ prevents mistakes from hiding — you get an immediate error.
The order of reading code is no longer important.
cons: var returning undefined creates silent bugs.
Arrow functions and function expressions are not hoisted — this causes confusion.
This behavior feels counter-intuitive for beginners.
gotchas: Only the declaration is hoisted, not the assignment. That is the core point.
function f(){} is fully hoisted, but var f = function(){} hoists only the var f part.
class is also in the TDZ — you cannot new it before declaration.
terms: Before execution JS lifts all declarations to the top — not the values.
Temporal Dead Zone — the portion from the start of a block until the declaration where let/const cannot be accessed.
where: The answer to "where did undefined come from?" is often hoisting.
You can write a function declaration later and still call it earlier — common for helper functions.
TDZ and "what is hoisted and what is not" are asked directly.
hoisting.visualCap: All three are hoisted — but var gets undefined, let/const are in the TDZ, and functions are fully prepared.

=== is straightforward: type same + value same, only then true.

== first coerces types to be the same, then compares. This "coercion first" is where everything goes wrong.
equality.why: There is only one real place where == is useful: x == null — it catches both null and undefined together. Use === everywhere else.
pros: === behavior is always predictable.

Object.is handles NaN and -0 edge cases correctly.

=== also compares object references, not content.
NaN's behavior is odd and easy to forget.

[] == false is true but if ([]) works — the two rules differ.
In an interview, when asked "Do you ever use ==?", answer: "Only for x == null."

Like ===, but handles NaN and -0 correctly.
where: Default is always ===. Keep the eqeqeq rule on in your linter.
if (x == null) — checks both in one line.

nullish.q: What is the difference between null, undefined, and NaN? How do you reliably check for each?
nullish.what:
All three appear as “nothing”, but their meaning is different:

undefined = “no one gave a value”. null = “I intentionally left it empty”. NaN = “tried to make a number, couldn’t”.
nullish.analogy: A form field. undefined = field hasn't been displayed yet. null = field displayed, user entered "N/A". NaN = user entered "abc" for age.
nullish.why: The difference matters because undefined is often a bug (“no value arrived”) and null is often valid (“empty is okay”). In API design too: returning null means “searched, not found”; undefined means “maybe I never looked”.
pros: ?? and ?. have made this whole area easy.
Having two distinct meanings makes the code’s intent clear.
With x == null both are checked together.
cons: The typeof null returning "object" still confuses.
Having two “empty” values is considered a design flaw.
NaN is not equal to itself.
gotchas: Difference between || and ??: || provides a default for every falsy value, ?? only for null/undefined.
typeof null === "object" — to identify, write x === null.
If a function has no return, it returns undefined, not null.
terms: No value was given — JavaScript assigns it automatically.
Value was intentionally left empty — you assigned it.
Not a Number — the numeric operation failed.
where: Use ??, not || — otherwise 0 and "" would also be replaced.
A field being null means “empty”; undefined means “not present”.
obj?.a?.b avoids crashes without a long if chain.

scope.q: Explain the three types of scope in JavaScript with examples.
scope.what:
Three types of areas exist: global (entire file), function (inside a function), and block (inside a { } — only for let/const).

When JavaScript needs a variable, it looks from inside outward — in its own scope, then the next outer scope, then up to global. This is called the scope chain.
scope.analogy: Finding something in a house: first in your own room, if not found then in the hall, if still not found then in the whole house. It never works backward — someone in the hall cannot open the cupboard in your room.
scope.why: Without it, every variable would be global and variables from two functions would clash. Scope is what makes closures possible — and from it come this, hoisting, and the module pattern.
pros: Variables don’t clash — each function has its own area.
Block scope prevents for loop and if variables from leaking.
The global namespace stays clean.
cons: In deep nesting, finding “where this variable came from” is difficult.
If the scope chain is long, lookup is slightly slower (practically negligible).
var’s function scope still causes confusion in legacy code.
gotchas: Lexical means: scope is determined by the place where it is written, not where it is called.
var does not respect block scope — it is visible throughout the entire function even inside an if.
Creating a variable without let/const/var makes it global (error in strict mode).
terms: The area where a variable is visible.
If a variable isn’t found, JS searches the outer scopes — up to global.
Scope is decided by the place where the code is written, not where it is executed.
where: A closure sits on the entire scope chain — without it, things don’t make sense.
Different functions can use a variable with the same name without conflict.
Keeping everything inside a function keeps the global scope clean.
scope.visualCap: Lookup always goes from inner to outer, never the reverse. Therefore inner can see outer, but outer cannot see inner.

closures.qsub: How does the classic loop-with-setTimeout bug demonstrate closures? How do you fix it?
closures.what:
If you create a function inside another function, the inner one can see the outer function’s variables. That’s normal.

The amazing part is that even after the outer function has finished, the inner function remembers those variables. They don’t disappear. That’s called a closure.
closures.analogy: When you leave the office for home, you put a file in a bag. The office shuts down — but the file is still in the bag. Function = you, bag = closure.
closures.why: JavaScript didn’t have anything like private. So how do you create data that only certain functions can access? Closures provide the solution — keep the variable inside, expose only the necessary functions outside.
pros: True private data — there was no other way in JS.
A new, separate bag on each call — two counters don’t interfere with each other.
Eliminates the need for global variables.
cons: It doesn’t release memory while the closure is alive.
The classic bug with loops + var (see below).
Deep nesting can be hard to read.
gotchas: for (var i=0;i<3;i++) setTimeout(()=>log(i)) prints 3 three times — var is a single variable. Use let.
A closure doesn’t keep a copy of the value; it keeps a reference — if the value changes later, the new value will be seen.
In an interview, don’t just give the definition — also mention a real use case (e.g., debounce or useState).
terms: The region where a variable is visible.
A function that remembers its outer variables even after the outer function has finished.
where: useState relies on closures — each component remembers its own state.
The timer ID lives in the closure, so each debounce has its own timer.
Module pattern — secret cannot be accessed from outside.

execution-context.desc: JS creates a context for every function call; the call stack tracks the current execution chain.
execution-context.what:
Whenever a function runs, JS creates a new frame — it holds that function's variables, its scope chain, and its this.

These frames are placed in a stack. The topmost one is running; as soon as it finishes it is removed and the one below moves forward.
execution-context.analogy: Placing books on a table. A new book is always placed on top and taken from the top. You can't pull one out from the middle.
execution-context.why: The stack trace shown in an error is this same stack. And "Maximum call stack size exceeded" means the stack grew so tall that it collapsed (infinite recursion).
pros: Order is always predictable — no race condition.
You can reach the bug directly from the stack trace.
Memory is automatically freed when a frame is removed.
cons: Deep recursion causes stack overflow (~10k calls).
A heavy function blocks the entire page.
Async code breaks the stack trace — debugging becomes difficult.
gotchas: "Maximum call stack size exceeded" always means infinite recursion — check the base case.
Stack trace is read backwards — the topmost line was the last to execute.
Using a loop instead of recursion eliminates the stack limit problem.
terms: A frame that tells: which code is currently running, what its variables are, and what this is.
The stack of these frames. The topmost one is currently running.
where: DevTools' "Call Stack" panel shows this — the fastest way to reach a bug.
Each recursive call creates a new frame — therefore there is a depth limit.
The event loop picks up something only when this stack is empty.
execution-context.visualCap: Each function call creates a new frame. The topmost one finishes first — that's why the error stack trace is read backwards.

this.desc: this refers to the object that is executing the current function — its value depends on call context.
this.q: Explain how this is determined. What are the four rules of binding?
this.what:
The value of this is not determined by writing the function — it is determined when the function is called. This single line clears all confusion.

The same function called from different places will give a different this.
this.analogy: "Main" word is similar. Who is speaking changes the meaning — the word stays the same. this is the same: its value changes depending on who calls it.
this.why: Thousands of objects share the same method — the method’s code exists in one place. Therefore the method needs to know which object’s data to use. The answer is this.
pros: A single method’s code can be shared by thousands of objects.
Arrow functions have almost eliminated the callback this problem.
Using call/apply/bind gives full control over this.
cons: The value is determined at call time — hard to guess by reading.
When a method is assigned to a variable, this breaks.
Arrow and regular functions have opposite behavior — confusion is common.
gotchas: Arrow functions do not have their own this — they inherit it from where they are defined. Therefore, do not use an arrow for an object method.
const fn = obj.method; fn() — this is lost. This is the most common bug.
In an interview, list the four rules (new → call/bind → dot → standalone) — that is the complete answer.

The place from which the function is called — this determines this.
where: In React class components, you had to bind this.handleClick — that’s why.
When you pass a method as a callback, this is lost — you need an arrow function or .bind().
In addEventListener, the this of a normal function is the element itself.

hof.desc: Functions that take other functions as arguments or return them — the basis of functional JS.
hof.what:
In JavaScript a function is a normal value — you can store it in a variable, pass it as an argument, or return it.

A function that takes another function or returns one is called a higher-order function. map, filter, setTimeout, addEventListener — all are examples.
hof.why: Without it you have to write a full loop for every small task. HOF separates the "what to do" from "how to iterate" — and that makes the code smaller and more readable.
pros: Loop boilerplate disappears — the intent is clear.
You can chain, and each step can be tested separately.
Reusable — the same map works on any kind of data.

Too much chaining becomes hard to read.

currying.qsub: What is the difference between currying and partial application?
currying.what:
Turning add(a, b, c) into add(a)(b)(c) — that's currying.

The benefit is that you can pre-fill some arguments ahead of time and create a new, smaller function.
currying.analogy: Tea order: "one tea, less sugar, with ginger". Currying means you first say "less sugar, with ginger" — now each time you only need to say "one tea".
currying.why: When the same setting repeats over and over, fill it once and create a new function. This removes code duplication.
pros: Fill repeating arguments once.
Create small, specific functions and give them names.
Makes composition easier.

Each step creates a new function — a bit of overhead.
Debugging is hard — anonymous functions appear in the stack.

iife.desc: A function that runs the moment it is defined — used to create isolated scope.
iife.qsub: How does an IIFE prevent polluting the global scope?
iife.what:
A function that runs immediately as soon as it is written: (function(){ ... })().

Its sole purpose was—to create its own scope, so that the inner variables do not end up in the global scope.
iife.why:
Before let/const and ES modules, the only way to create a scope was a function. So they would wrap the entire file in a function.

Today its need is almost gone — block scope and modules have taken over this job. But you will find it everywhere in old code and library bundles, so recognizing it is important.
pros: Keeps the global namespace clean.
A clean way to run one-time setup code.
Provides private data via closure.
cons: Almost unnecessary today — let/block/modules are sufficient.
The syntax feels heavy to read.
Unnamed functions appear as "anonymous" in debugging.
gotchas: If the previous line does not end with a semicolon, the IIFE’s leading ( is taken as a function call — a classic ASI bug.
There is no need to write IIFEs in new code today — mentioning this in an interview is a good signal.
An IIFE does not itself provide private data — that comes from a closure. The IIFE only creates a scope.
terms: Immediately Invoked Function Expression — a function that runs as soon as it is defined.
A separate area so that names do not clash in the global scope.
where: jQuery-era libraries were completely wrapped in IIFEs.
Webpack/Rollup output is still wrapped in an IIFE today.

event-loop.desc: The mechanism that lets JS be non-blocking: picks tasks from the queue when the call stack is empty.
event-loop.q: Explain the event loop. What is the difference between the microtask queue and macrotask queue?
event-loop.qsub: What is the order of output for: setTimeout, Promise.then, queueMicrotask?
event-loop.what:
JS can do only one thing at a time. So why doesn’t a 5-second network call freeze the page?

Because JS doesn’t do that work itself — it hands it off to the browser and moves on. When the response arrives it goes into a queue. The Event loop is the guard that keeps asking, "Is the stack empty? Then take the next item from the queue."
event-loop.analogy: Doctor (stack) sees one patient at a time. Sent a blood test to the lab, then saw the next patient. When the report arrives it goes into the waiting line. And there are two lines — VIP (promises) and normal (setTimeout).
event-loop.why: Without it, every network call would freeze the entire page. And it’s important to understand because interview output-order questions and "why doesn’t my state update appear immediately?" — both are answered by this.
pros: Even with a single thread, the UI doesn’t freeze.
No race conditions, no locks — one piece of code runs at a time.
The order of promises is always deterministic.
cons: A heavy calculation can freeze the entire page.
setTimeout(fn, 0) does not mean "right now".
The output order seems confusing at first.
gotchas: setTimeout(fn, 0) does not run immediately — it’s queued, and the browser’s minimum is ~4 ms.
All code after await becomes a microtask — so the outer next queue runs first.
In an interview, don’t just say "it takes from the queue" — mention the two queues and their order.
terms: The stack of work that is currently executing. One at a time.
where: Every frontend interview includes an output-order question — it follows exactly this rule.
"Why does the old value appear immediately after setState?" — because React puts it in the update queue.
A heavy loop keeps the stack busy, preventing the browser from painting.
event-loop.visualCap: The most important rule: after each macrotask, the entire microtask queue must be empty — only then does the next macrotask run.

callbacks.what:
If JavaScript has to do some long-running task (network, file, timer), it doesn't stop and wait. You give it a function: "run this when it's done". That's a callback.

The problem arises when one task follows another, then a third — each one goes inside the other.
callbacks.why: Callback hell wasn't just ugly in appearance — error handling was its real pain. You had to check errors separately at each level, and if you missed one, the error disappeared silently. Promises came as the answer to this pain.
pros: The simplest idea — no extra concept.
Still the best approach for events.
Lighter than promises — no microtask overhead.
cons: Nesting makes the code tilt to the right.
Error has to be handled at every level.
It's easy to accidentally call a callback twice.
gotchas: In Node style, error is the first argument — (err, data). Forgetting this is a common mistake.
Throwing inside a callback is not caught by an outer try/catch.
To convert old callback APIs to promises, use util.promisify or a custom new Promise wrapper.

Callbacks inside callbacks — the code tilts to the right.

The function given to map, filter is also a callback (but sync).
Node's legacy APIs are all callback-based — it's important to recognize them.

promises.q: Explain how a Promise works internally. What are the three states?
promises.what:
A Promise is a receipt. The work hasn't finished yet, but you have something you can say "let me know when it’s done".

It has three states: pending (in progress), fulfilled (completed, has a value), rejected (failed, has an error). Once settled it is settled forever — it never changes.
promises.analogy: Laundry receipt. The clothes aren't here yet, but you have the receipt. Clothes arrive = fulfilled. Clothes lost = rejected. And once it’s decided it cannot change.
promises.why: Promise fixed the two biggest pains of callbacks: nesting (the chain runs straight down) and error handling (a single .catch() handles the entire chain).
pros: Chain runs straight down — nesting eliminated.
A single .catch() handles errors for the whole chain.
Combinators (all, race) make parallel work easy.
cons: Once started you cannot cancel it (AbortController is needed separately).
Forgetting return inside .then breaks the chain — silently.
Nested promises can still be written — the promise does not flatten automatically.
gotchas: It is essential to place a return inside .then — otherwise the next step receives undefined.
A Promise starts executing immediately upon creation — it doesn’t wait for .then.
If you forget to add .catch, you get an "unhandled rejection" — and in Node that can crash the process.
terms: A container that says "the answer isn’t ready yet, but it will be — either a value or an error".
Three states. Once it leaves pending, it never changes.
.then() always returns a new promise — that’s why a chain forms.
where: fetch() returns a promise — every API call uses this.
It’s a thin wrapper over promises — the same thing runs underneath.
promises.visualCap: Once it leaves pending it is settled forever. .then builds a chain, and if any step fails it jumps straight to .catch.

async-await.q: How does async/await work under the hood? What does await actually do?
async-await.what:
async/await is not a new thing — it is a small syntax over promises. The same promises run underneath.

await means: "pause here, continue when the result arrives". But it does not stop the whole program — only this function pauses; the rest of the code keeps running.
async-await.why: Reading a promise chain was fine, but loops and if-else inside it became awkward. With await, async code starts looking exactly like normal synchronous code — try/catch works again as usual.
pros: Async code becomes readable like synchronous code.
try/catch, loops, if-else — all work normally.
Debugger step-through works correctly.
cons: Writing await one after another makes the code unnecessarily slow.
Every async function returns a promise — if you forget, [object Promise] gets printed.
Top-level await works only in ES modules.
gotchas: Biggest mistake: awaiting items one by one that could run in parallel. Use Promise.all.
await does not work inside forEach — use for...of.
Calling an async function without await and it fails will result in an "unhandled rejection".
terms: Makes the function return a promise.
Waits for the promise's result — but does not block the thread.
where: All data fetching is written this way today.
When the next step depends on the previous step's result.

promise-combinators.why: Writing await one by one makes the work unnecessarily slow — three API calls that could run in parallel will take three times the time. Combinators are the solution for this. And allSettled fixes another pain: if one widget fails, the whole page should not crash.

Wait for everyone, even if they fail — give results for all.
Whichever finishes first (success or failure) provides the answer.
First to succeed. Fails only if all fail.
where: Multiple APIs together — use allSettled so that if one fails, the others can still be shown.
Use race to set a time limit on a network call.
Use any to pick the first working mirror.

generators.desc: Functions that can pause and resume execution using yield — the foundation of async/await internals.
generators.what:
Normal function runs once and stops only after completing. Generator (function*) can pause in the middle — at yield.

And the most useful point: who holds the pause? The outside. You call next(), then it moves forward.
generators.analogy: A Netflix series. You watch one episode (yield), paused. You press "next" and then the next one plays. The whole series doesn’t run all at once.
generators.why: Two main purposes: infinite or large sequences (providing values one by one without creating a full array), and the underlying mechanism of async/await — async/await is actually built from generators + promises.
pros: Lazy — value is created only when requested. Saves memory.
Infinite sequences possible.
Key to understanding how async/await works.
cons: Syntax is not common — not everyone on the team understands it.
In most cases async/await is sufficient.
Debugging is hard — control jumps back and forth.
gotchas: function* invocation does not run the code — it only returns an iterator. The first next() starts it.
With next(value) you can also send a value into the generator — yield becomes its result.
Once a generator is finished (done: true) it cannot be restarted — you need to create a new one.

The point where the function pauses and yields a value outward.
An object that has a next() method which returns {value, done}.
where: Large data – processing each record one by one without building a full array.
Infinite sequence – ID generator, Fibonacci — generates as much as needed.
Redux-Saga – the entire library is built on generators.

microtask-macrotask.desc: Microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) run before the next macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval).
microtask-macrotask.q: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks? Predict the output of a tricky async snippet.
microtask-macrotask.what:
There are two separate queues, and their rule in one line: run one macrotask → empty the entire microtask queue → then the next macrotask.

Therefore Promise.then always runs before setTimeout(fn, 0), even if setTimeout is written first.
microtask-macrotask.why: The microtask queue was created so that the promise's response arrives before the next paint. Otherwise each .then would be a whole frame late and the UI would flicker.
pros: Promises' order is always fixed and predictable.
Microtasks run before paint — the UI appears correct immediately.
A single mental model lets you understand the entire async order.
cons: A microtask chain can starve the page (starvation).
You have to remember two queues.
Node's model is a bit different (process.nextTick, phases).
gotchas: process.nextTick (Node) runs before microtasks — it’s a separate queue.
To split heavy work you need setTimeout (macro) — breaking with a microtask prevents the browser from painting.
In an interview, the answer to “what is a microtask” is: after a macrotask the entire microtask queue is emptied — that line alone is enough.
terms: If microtasks never finish, macrotasks never run — the page hangs.
where: Output-order questions come directly from this.
Microtask to read right after a DOM update; requestAnimationFrame for the next frame.
If you need to split a large task, use setTimeout so the browser can paint.

prototype-chain.q: Explain the prototype chain. How does property lookup work in JavaScript?
prototype-chain.qsub: What is the difference between __proto__ and prototype?
prototype-chain.what:
In JS every object has a hidden link — to its prototype. When you ask for obj.foo and it isn't on the object, JS follows that link. Not found there either, then further up. Until null.

This chain is called the prototype chain. This is JS's inheritance.
prototype-chain.analogy: If you don’t find something at home, you ask the neighbor; if they don’t have it, you ask their neighbor. Eventually you reach a place where there’s no one ahead (null)—then you get undefined.
prototype-chain.why: That’s why every array has map without it being defined on each one. map lives in one place on Array.prototype—thousands of arrays share it. Memory is saved.
pros: Methods are in one place—thousands of objects share them, saving memory.
Behavior can be added at runtime.
More flexible than class-based inheritance.
cons: Longer chain lookups are slightly slower.
Modifying built-in prototypes (monkey-patching) is dangerous.
People coming from class-based languages find it confusing.
gotchas: __proto__ and prototype are different: __proto__ exists on an object, prototype exists on a function.
for...in also iterates over inherited properties—Object.keys() does not.
Don’t add your own method to Array.prototype—it will appear on every array and can break libraries.
terms: An object that other objects keep as a "if not found here, look here" reference.
The object's link to its prototype.
The property of a function that becomes the prototype of objects created with new.
where: class internally uses this chain—it’s just nicer syntax.
In DevTools, opening [[Prototype]] shows the entire chain.
prototype-chain.visualCap: The chain runs from inside to outside. map isn’t on the array, it’s on Array.prototype—and thousands of arrays share that single copy.

class.q: Are JavaScript classes "real" classes? What is happening under the hood?
class.qsub: What is the difference between a class expression and declaration? What are static methods?
class.what:
class in JavaScript doesn't bring anything new. It's the same prototype chain, only the syntax is cleaner.

class Dog { bark(){} } actually creates Dog.prototype.bark.
class.why: The old prototype syntax (Dog.prototype.bark = function...) was scattered and setting up inheritance required a 4-5 line workaround. class cleaned that up — and also introduced new benefits like # private fields that previously were only possible with closures.
pros: Much cleaner syntax than the prototype workaround.
You get true private fields with #.
Inheritance is straightforward with extends/super.
cons: People think this is a Java-like class — it isn’t; it’s still prototype-based.
In JavaScript, plain objects plus functions are often sufficient.
Deep hierarchies become heavy quickly in JavaScript.
gotchas: Classes are hoisted but remain in the TDZ — you cannot new them before they are declared.
Class code always runs in strict mode, even if you didn’t write "use strict".
When you assign a method to a variable, this is lost — avoid this with arrow class fields (fn = () => {}).
terms: A clean syntax for prototype-based inheritance. Internally it still uses prototypes.
Not new functionality, just a better way to write existing behavior.
True private field — cannot be accessed from outside.
where: Data and its rules in one place — validation, computed values.

inheritance.desc: JS uses object-to-object delegation, not class-to-instance. extends sets up the prototype chain.
inheritance.q: Explain the difference between prototypal and classical inheritance. When is composition better?
inheritance.what:
In Java, a class is a blueprint and objects are created from it. In JavaScript, an object directly takes things from another object — there is no blueprint in between.

class ... extends looks like Java, but inside the same prototype linking is happening.
inheritance.why:
Understanding the difference is important because in JavaScript you can change the prototype at runtime, and you can create an object directly from another object — this is not possible in Java.

And practical advice: avoid deep inheritance in JavaScript. Composition (adding things together) is often better.
pros: Prototype can be changed even at runtime.
You can create an object directly from another object — without a class.
Very flexible when combined with composition.
cons: Reading and debugging a deep chain is difficult.
When the same logic is needed in two places, composition is the way.
setPrototypeOf used at runtime degrades performance.
gotchas: extends needs super() first — before using this.
Object.create(null) creates an object with no prototype — best for a pure dictionary.
In an interview: "JS has no classical inheritance, it is prototypal with syntax sugar" — this answer is strong.

Class to class — the Java/C++ style. This is not native in JavaScript.
Building by adding things together instead of inheritance.
where: extends Error — the clearest, most common use of inheritance.
React.Component, custom HTML elements — inheritance is necessary.
Mixins/composition — when behavior is needed from multiple places.

new-keyword.desc: Creates a blank object, sets its prototype, runs the constructor with this, and returns the object.
new-keyword.q: What does the new keyword do step by step? What happens if a constructor returns an object?
new-keyword.what:
new Foo() applied, JS does four things, in that order:

1. Creates an empty object.
2. Sets that object's prototype to Foo.prototype.
3. Executes Foo with this = that new object.
4. Returns the object (unless the function itself returns an object).
new-keyword.why: Knowing these four steps is important because every bug can be traced back to them. Forgetting new makes this incorrect, you learn how the prototype is linked, and what happens when a constructor returns an object — all answers are in this list. This is asked directly in interviews.
pros: One consistent method everywhere — the standard for creating objects.
The prototype is automatically linked.
You can catch incorrect usage with new.target.
cons: Forgetting new silently creates bugs (in non-strict mode).
Returning an object from the constructor changes the behavior — confusing.
It doesn't work with arrow functions at all.
gotchas: If the constructor returns an object, it overrides this. If it returns a primitive, it is ignored.
Calling a class without new always throws an error — the constructor function would otherwise run silently.
You cannot use new on an arrow function — it has no prototype.
terms: Runs the function as a constructor and creates a new object.
The function that is called with new.
where: Classes and constructor functions — both are invoked with new.
"What does new do under the hood" is asked directly — list the four steps.

object-methods.desc: Built-in methods to create, copy, and lock down objects at the property descriptor level.
object-methods.q: What is the difference between Object.freeze and Object.seal? When would you use each?
object-methods.what: Four utilities that are useful with objects daily — and the three freeze/seal ones work only at the top level.
object-methods.why: These four utilities are useful daily — but their shallow nature is the biggest trap. People apply Object.freeze and assume the whole object is safe, while the nested object inside can still be changed. Therefore, it's essential to know their limits before using them.

freeze prevents accidental changes.
You can run map/filter on an object using entries/fromEntries.

freeze is somewhat expensive on large objects.

Object.assign invokes getters and copies the returned value — the getter itself is not copied.

mixins.q: What is a mixin in JavaScript? How does it solve the diamond problem of multiple inheritance?
mixins.what:
In JS a class can have only one parent. But often you need behaviour from two or three places.

A mixin is the workaround: keep the behaviour in a plain object or function, and mix it in to whoever needs it.
mixins.why: The classic pain of inheritance: ElectricCar, FlyingCar, ElectricFlyingCar... each combination requires its own class. With mixins, creating a combination becomes like attaching, not like building a new class.
pros: Avoids the single-parent limit.
Creating combinations is cheap — no need to create a new class.
Small, separate pieces — easier to test.
cons: Names can clash — if two mixins have the same method, one silently overwrites the other.
"Where did this method come from?" becomes hard to trace.
Too many mixins cause the class behavior to become scattered.
gotchas: Object.assign(Class.prototype, mixin) silently overwrites existing methods — no warning.
Keeping state (fields) in a mixin is dangerous — all instances can share it.
Often simple composition (storing an object in a field) is cleaner than a mixin — think about that first.
terms: A piece of behavior that can be mixed into many classes/objects.
Building things by composing rather than using inheritance.
where: Logging, serialization, events — many classes need it.
Mixins were its core feature (Vue 3 replaced them with the composition API).
Turning a class into an event emitter without inheritance.

garbage-collection.what:
In JS you don't free memory — the engine does. Its rule is simple: any object that is no longer reachable will be cleaned up.

Reachable means: global, current stack, or there is a path from any reachable object to it.
garbage-collection.analogy: Household items: anything that someone is holding onto stays. Anything no one is holding goes to the trash. It's not about "is it old" — it's about "is anyone still holding onto it".

memory-leaks.what:
A leak does not mean "memory is full" — it means someone is holding onto something that is no longer needed.

In JavaScript there are only four major causes, and all four are recognizable.
memory-leaks.why: This is the biggest issue in SPAs. The page does not reload, so with each screen change a small amount of leak accumulates — and after an hour the app becomes slow or crashes.

debounce-throttle.q: What is the difference between debounce and throttle? Implement both from scratch.
debounce-throttle.what:
Both aim to reduce repeatedly running work — but the logic is opposite:

Debounce: "as long as events keep coming, I will stay idle. When they stop I will run."
Throttle: "I will definitely run once every X ms, regardless of how many events arrive."
debounce-throttle.why: Without them, a search box would send an API call on every keystroke and scrolling would trigger calculations on every frame — both make the app slow and put unnecessary load on the server. These two small functions are the cure for that whole pain, and both rely on closures (where the timer is stored — that same closure).
pros: API calls and re-renders are greatly reduced.
Both can be written in about 10 lines yourself (often asked in interviews).
The clearest real-world use of closures.
cons: With debounce the user experiences a delay.
Choosing the wrong one makes the behavior feel opposite.
In React a new debounce is created on every render — useMemo/useRef are needed.
gotchas: Selection rule: need the final value → debounce. Need intermediate updates as well → throttle.
In React, creating debounce without useMemo will generate a new one on each render and it won’t work.
When the component unmounts, you must call clearTimeout — otherwise setState may run on an unmounted component.

At most once per interval — no matter how much the user acts.
where: Debounce — avoid an API call on every keystroke.
Throttle — avoid calculating on every frame.
Throttle — send only one request per button press.

lazy-evaluation.desc: Deferring computation until the value is actually needed — generators, Proxy, and on-demand patterns.
lazy-evaluation.what:
Lazy means: don't calculate until someone asks for it.

In JS this already exists in many places — short-circuit &&/||, generators, and dynamic import().
lazy-evaluation.why: In large apps, most code is never used by the user. If you load everything upfront, the page will take longer to open. Lazy thinking says: fetch only what is needed now, the rest when requested. This is why modern apps are split into smaller bundles.
pros: Useless work never happens.
Initial load becomes very fast.
Infinite sequences become possible.
cons: Work happens later — the user sees a delay at that time.
Debugging is hard — "when did this run?"
Being overly lazy makes the code harder to understand.
gotchas: In a || b(), b() never runs if a is truthy — don’t place side effects there.
To lazy-load, pass a function, not a value — passing a value causes it to be calculated immediately.

try-catch.desc: try/catch/finally is JS error handling. catch blocks receive the error object. finally always runs (even after return). Errors propagate up the call stack if uncaught. throw can re-throw or throw new errors.
try-catch.qsub: What is the difference between throw new Error() and just throw? When would you re-throw?
try-catch.what:
When a throw occurs, the function stops right there and the error climbs upward — to the caller that invoked it. If there is no catch there either, it goes further up. If it is not caught anywhere, the program crashes.

finally always runs — whether an error occurs or not, even if a return happens.
try-catch.why: For cleanup, finally is the right place — stop a loader, close a connection, release a lock. Because it runs on every path: normal execution, error, and early return.

Cleanup is guaranteed with finally.

Swallowing errors (empty catch) is the most dangerous habit.

Don’t leave an empty catch {} — at least log something, otherwise the bug stays hidden forever.

The error propagates upward until someone catches it.

async-errors.qsub: What is the difference between an unhandled rejection and an uncaught exception? How does React Error Boundary handle async errors?
async-errors.what:
Async errors behave differently from sync errors, and this creates the most bugs.

Two rules: (1) a throw inside a callback does not reach the outer try/catch. (2) If a Promise does not have a .catch, the error silently disappears (and in Node the process crashes).
async-errors.why: Sync errors crash the program — they are visible. Async errors silently disappear. This is why the most hidden bugs in production are async errors, and therefore a rule to use either await or .catch on every promise must be established.
pros: async/await makes normal try/catch work again.
Global handlers provide a final safety net.

Never write forEach(async ...) — use for...of or Promise.all.

The final net — errors that were not caught anywhere end up here.

Normal Map holds onto its keys. So if the key is a DOM node and it is removed from the page, it will still remain in memory — because Map keeps it.
